analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax credits for private health insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the Affordable Care Act and replaced it with tax credits for private insurance, was referred to ten House committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have wiped out the Affordable Care Act entirely, then rebuilt coverage around a refundable tax credit for low-income people buying private insurance, a tax deduction for everyone else, association health plans for individuals and small businesses, and the ability to buy insurance across state lines. Unlike the law it repealed, it would not have required insurers to cover everyone or charge sick and healthy people the same rates. It also let Medicare patients pay doctors directly outside standard Medicare rules, exempted doctors from antitrust laws when negotiating with insurers, capped children's CHIP coverage at 300% of the poverty line, and allowed premiums to vary by up to 50% based on wellness-program participation.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured people would gain a refundable tax credit for private coverage (capped at $2,000 per adult plus $500 per child, covering at most two dependents, phasing out above 200% of the poverty line). Higher-income and healthy people would gain from a new deduction for insurance costs and from insurers being freed to price policies by health status. Physicians would gain an antitrust exemption for bargaining with insurers, the right to contract privately with Medicare patients outside standard Medicare payment rules, and a higher burden of proof in malpractice suits. Insurers and business associations would gain new sales channels through association health plans and interstate sales with fewer state mandates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Healthy buyers, physicians, insurers, small businesses

how_it_helps.text: It created a refundable tax credit for the cost of health insurance for low-income taxpayers, phasing down from 100% starting at 200% of the poverty line, with an option to receive it in advance as premium payments.
It let all other taxpayers deduct the cost of their health insurance premiums.

It expanded pooling options: individual and small-employer membership associations and federally certified association health plans under ERISA, letting individuals and small businesses band together to buy coverage.

It appropriated $300 million a year for fiscal 2014–2016 for state high-risk pools and reinsurance mechanisms to subsidize private coverage for people whose medical conditions make them uninsurable at standard rates.

It allowed Medicare beneficiaries to contract directly with a physician, freed doctors from antitrust laws when negotiating contract terms with health plans, and made compliance with federal best-practice guidelines a factor in malpractice lawsuits.
It created loan funds for medical students and loan forgiveness for primary-care providers to address physician shortages, and funded fraud enforcement at HHS.

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions would bear the largest cost: with no guaranteed-issue or community-rating requirement, insurers could deny them coverage or charge unaffordable rates. Children in families above 300% of the poverty line would lose CHIP eligibility. Medicare beneficiaries who see doctors choosing to contract privately could be billed above Medicare rates, since states would be barred from limiting what those providers charge. Patients suing for malpractice would face a changed burden of proof, and people unable to participate in wellness programs could pay up to 50% more in premiums and cost-sharing. States would lose authority over insurance sold across their borders.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and seniors

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly provided no mandate for guaranteed issue or community rating (Sec. 3), so insurers could once again deny coverage or charge much higher premiums to people with pre-existing conditions — the group the Affordable Care Act's rules were written to protect.
It prohibited CHIP payments for children in families with income above 300% of the poverty line, reducing children's health coverage relative to existing law.

It let Medicare beneficiaries contract privately with physicians and barred states from limiting what those providers charge, meaning doctors could bill patients above Medicare rates and seniors could face out-of-pocket charges they cannot negotiate.
It allowed group plans to vary premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50% based on wellness-program participation, which can raise costs for people whose jobs or health make participation impossible.
The low-income tax credit covers at most two dependents per family and phases out starting at 200% of the poverty line, leaving gaps for larger low-income families just above that threshold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered genuine help to some: refundable tax credits for low-income people buying private coverage, loan forgiveness for primary-care doctors, and federal grants for state high-risk pools. But the honest cost was large: with no guaranteed-issue or community-rating mandate (Sec. 3), insurers could again deny coverage or set premiums based on health, the wellness provision allowed premiums to vary by up to 50% based on program participation, CHIP help for children was cut off above 300% of poverty, and the Medicare contracting provision let providers bill seniors above Medicare rates by overriding state limits. The design shifted risk from insurers and providers onto the people least able to bear it, while the replacement subsidies were far narrower than the programs they would have replaced.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to ten House committees and then to four subcommittees, none of which ever voted to send it to the floor, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tom Price of Georgia introduced the bill on June 6, 2013, and it was referred the same day to ten House committees, led by Energy and Commerce.

Within six weeks it had been sent to four subcommittees — Health, Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, Workforce Protections, and Constitution and Civil Justice — and no committee or subcommittee ever reported it out or held a recorded vote on it.
No chamber of Congress ever voted on the bill, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
Because the bill never became law, the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansions and insurance-market rules remained in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No law changed: the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansions and insurance rules — including protections for people with pre-existing conditions — remained in place, so the people who rely on those rules were better off that the bill died. Its supporters gained nothing beyond the bill's 60 Republican endorsements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People protected by the Affordable Care Act's rules

for.name: Rep. Tom Price
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 6, 2013 as a full repeal-and-replace of the Affordable Care Act.

for.name: 59 of 234 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 59 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and nine other committees of referral
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral; no committee ever voted the bill out for a floor vote.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority (55 seats)
against.role: Senate majority under Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV)
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate, opposed repealing the Affordable Care Act, and gave the bill no consideration there.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — the sponsor and all 59 cosponsors were House Republicans — while the Democratic-run Senate never took it up.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the Affordable Care Act's guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules and its benefit mandates, letting them again deny or price coverage based on health; the bill's tax credits would also keep public subsidies flowing through private insurance plans as the permanent channel for coverage.

The bill exempts doctors from antitrust laws when bargaining with health plans, lets them contract privately with Medicare patients outside standard payment rules, bars states from limiting what they can charge, and raises the burden of proof in malpractice suits — each shifting bargaining power and billing freedom toward providers.

industries.industry: Business associations and chambers of commerce sponsoring health plans
industries.note: New association health plans and membership associations under ERISA would let trade groups and chambers sell coverage across regulatory lines, creating a new business line at the cost of weaker state consumer-protection oversight.
